analysis.one_liner: Bans consumer drug ads for the first three years after a drug's approval.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop pharmaceutical companies from advertising new prescription drugs directly to consumers for three years after FDA approval, so that safety problems have time to surface before mass marketing begins. The FDA could allow ads in the third year if they would help public health, and could extend the ban beyond three years if a drug turns out to have serious side effects.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, who would be less likely to be pushed toward a newly approved drug before its long-term risks are known; doctors, who would face less pressure from patients asking for heavily advertised drugs; and consumers generally, since drug advertising drives demand for expensive brand-name drugs.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits direct-to-consumer advertising of a new drug during the first three years after FDA approval, so marketing cannot outpace evidence about a drug's real-world safety. [S2] [S3]

It lets the FDA extend the advertising ban beyond three years for drugs that show significant adverse health effects in post-approval studies, adverse event reports, or the scientific literature. [S2] [S3]
It allows a waiver for the third year only if the drug maker shows the FDA that advertising the drug would affirmatively benefit public health. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies, which would lose three years of consumer advertising for every new drug; television networks and other media outlets that carry drug ads; and advertising agencies. Some patients might also learn about new treatments later than they otherwise would.

drawbacks.text: Direct-to-consumer ads can inform patients about treatable conditions and prompt doctor visits; a three-year blackout could delay some patients from learning about new therapies. [S3]
The bill gives the FDA new case-by-case work — reviewing waiver applications and deciding which drugs warrant extended bans — with no added resources provided. [S3]
It applies only to drugs approved under the main new-drug pathway (section 505(b)) and only to drugs approved from a year before enactment forward, leaving some products untouched. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving new drugs a real-world safety track record before they are marketed to millions of viewers — addresses a documented problem: drugs are sometimes marketed heavily and withdrawn later when harms emerge. The costs are real but modest: advertisers and networks lose revenue, some patients hear about new drugs later, and the FDA takes on added review work. The bill's main weakness is that it drew no cosponsors and never received serious consideration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in February 2016, and neither ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 12, 2016. [S1] [S5]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and a week later to that committee's Health Subcommittee. [S5]
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies keep the ability to advertise newly approved drugs to consumers immediately, and the broadcasters and advertising firms that earn revenue from drug ads keep that revenue. Patients gained nothing from this outcome.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban consumer drug advertising for the first three years after approval.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (114th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 12, 2016 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry whose products the bill would regulate
against.what_they_did: The bill would have cost drug makers three years of direct-to-consumer advertising for every new drug; no industry or member support for the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill bars consumer ads for new drugs during their first three years on the market, cutting off a marketing channel that drives demand for expensive brand-name prescriptions — costs that flow to patients and insurers.

industries.industry: Broadcast TV networks and advertising industry
industries.note: Pharmaceutical consumer ads are a major source of television advertising revenue; a three-year delay for every new drug would shrink that revenue stream.
